newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China on target for leaded gasoline phase out.
newsitem.headline: China on target for leaded gasoline phase out.

text.p: Chinese consumption of unleaded gasoline has grown significantly, keeping it on target for the planned phase out of leaded gasoline by the end of 2000, a Chinese environmental specialist said on Thursday.

The use of unleaded gasoline grew to 60.4 percent in 1995 from 46 percent in 1992, Li Pei, a senior official at the Chinese National Environmental Protection Agency, told a conference on cleaner-burning motor fuels.
Li told Reuters in an interview after speaking ot the conference that the Chinese government would announce in November an action plan for the phasing out of leaded gasoline.

The plan would will outline steps to be taken for the production of new vehicles that can use unleaded gasoline and modifications to old ones as well as fiscal incentives to encourage the use of unleaded gasoline.
"Our automotive industry is changing the production of cars to use unleaded gasoline and have catalytic converters," she said.
Li said the oil industry was talking to the Ministry of Finance about tax incentives for the sale of unleaded petrol, which is now about 10 percent more expensive than leaded petrol.
In some countries, unleaded gasoline is taxed at a lower rate to encourage more motorist to use it.

In April, the official Xinhua news agency said China's major cities would introduce unleaded gasoline by 2000. The China Daily said earlier this month Beijing wwould ban the sale of leaded gasoline from June 1.

Li said the phasing out of leaded gasoline in Beijing would be done in phases. All 300 petrol stations in downtown Beijing would be refurbished over the next six months to sell only unleaded gasoline.
By the summer of 1998, all 800 stations in Beijing would be equipped to sell only unleaded petrol, she said.
Li also said the policy would be extended to other major cities and important tourists centres as well as special economic special zones by 1998 at the latest.
These include big cities such as Shanghai, Guangzhou and Tianjin and tourists cities such as Shenzen and Xiamen.
By the end of 2000, the production and use of leaded gasoline would be discountinued entirely, she said.

Li said Chinese laws on air pollution were amended in August 1995 so that "relevant competent departments shall devise plans for gradual decrease of lead gasoline production, until its production and usage discontinue."
As a result, several Chinese refineries have already refurbished their refineries to meet the growing demand for unleaded gasoline.
Beijing's largest gasoline supplier, Yanshan Petrochemical Corp, spent 1.1 billion yuan (132.5 million) on equipment renewal and began producing unleaded petrol in March.
Oil industry sources said China would have little difficulty meeting the new environmental standard as most large coastal refineries were equipped to produce high octane unleaded gasoline.
In the first quarter, China produced 8.06 million tonnes of gasoline and exported 504,112 tonnes, the bulk of it unleaded high octane gasoline, they said.
